Smoother and more polished than the original Phantasmagoria, this sequal is curiously absorbing, shifting the player from one scene to another seemlessly.  While the narrative has some issues sharpening the technical side of the tale; cultivating drama, suspence, and turmoil, Phantasmagoria 2 is an uncomplicated journey through the mind of a ordinary man trying to survive a meltdown caused by the trauma of his childhood; successfully finding the answers to why his life is hopelessly messed up.  Rated 7 out of 10.

After playing Phantasmagoria 1, this sequel feels like something you have to try. However, the bar set by the first game was simply too high for it to match. In my opinion, the story here is relatively weak, and the puzzles are quite easy to solve, with obvious hints scattered throughout the game. I really missed elements like the skull offering mysterious advice in a dark voice, as well as the secret passageways and the overall sense of mystery surrounding dark forces. That said, Phantasmagoria 2 does have solid gameplay mechanics, along with good video quality and performance. All things considered, it’s a decent game for its time. I’d give it a 6.5 out of 10, mostly because the story is weak and you can finish it in around three hours.

When FMV games first became a thing there was night trap ,sewer shark etc. Those types of game continuously played...not only did you often miss the story (especially with night trap as youre looking in different rooms), but it made them very limited with very small choices, basically just creating a different video playing. The first Phantasmagoria was a step forward where you controlled the player, Phantasmagoria 2 went further still. Although you still have premade videos (just like cutscenes in any game), you have MUCH more choice in the game , and it does make a difference to the ending......this was rare in the late 90s.

There is a genuine mystery here, all you know when the game starts is that you were in a strait jacket in hospital, and you begin the game with very little else as to who you are. The unravelling of the mystery is really well done. The characters are good and , for a first, some of the acting isnt bad at all (a rarity at the time). For me though, the excellent sets and ambiance steal the show. The videos are really close to the gameplay graphics in look and feel (the videos are real video and gameplay is kind of green screen super imposed people on photo like computer drawn scenes....its pretty seamless and very well done. The interaction with objects including the computer on your desk is also well done. A lot of thought went into making this an engrossing and interesting game.
         
The game is also quite long which surprised me. Ok the video is grainy and has greatly reduced quality and colour by todays standards, but it still does the job of drawing you into the game.

I wont spoil the game, but it has many characters, not all make it to the end , this increases interest, when people keep dying it just adds more mystery. I love that you can change the path of your character too.

This is , for me, the most interactive FMV game I have played......and Ive played most. Whilst there are others which are excellent too, nothing quite catches the depth and horror of a Puzzle of Flesh : Phantasmagoria 2.

I first got the game when it was released in the late 1990s back in the days of Pentium 2 computers and slow  hard drives.....its a joy to play with an ssd today. 

If you love a great horror like scifi story with a number of clever twists, great sets and quite often decent acting, you will love this game.
An easy recommend and one of the best of the genre.

Ken Williams produces this follow-up psycho-sexual/-patho/-logical horror FMV adventure game, featuring it's fair share of gore, paranoid intrigue, latex puppet effects, and BDSM dominatrices ready to stomp on your nethers.  

A year on from surviving a psychotic break with reality, our protagonist, Curtis, is gainfully employed at WynTech Industries, where he's practically ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all his co-workers between time spent trading witty barbs on the company clock.

It's a departure in design from your standard fair & its predecessor, in more ways than one.
The controls don't allow for much free-roaming or touch/taste/observe actions; but, instead, you click through various angles on real-world sets, while trying to highlight the appropriate pixels to interact with in the way the game has predetermined them.  At most, you'll combine inventory items, and maybe have the result interact with the environment or an NPC.

The FMV is comparatively top-notch, with very little of the janky bluescreen-based compositing that plagued the first entry in this mostly-unrelated duology.  Instead, this is very much an interactive movie, with the production values & cinematography to match that descriptor.
To its detriment, though, the game's 'puzzles' range from completely mundane -- like chatting with co-workers in their cubicles, or spending an hour making phone calls from your desk -- to the occasional outlandish action being required to advance -- like having your pet rat fetch items, like a dog.

The dialogue is incredibly dated, with a ton of references that you'd literally have to have lived through the mid-1990s to understand.
Everything from 'Beavis & Butthead' to the Clinton administration is lampooned in some fashion, which can adversely affect the approachability of the title.

Atmospherically, it's much closer to some Cronenbergian body-horror, by way of 'From Beyond', than a soap-opera-tier CGI creature feature -- which suits me just fine.

I'm several hours into the original Phantasmagoria and so far I prefer this one, A Puzzle of the Flesh.

Thematically, APoF deals with much more interesting subject matter: sexuality, class, and identity. If you don't care about the intellectual side of games, then it also has some great sequences and kills that you can only get from a game like this, from this particular era. For instance, one sequence involves getting into an S&M club dungeon, where your mild-mannered protagonist gets dommed by a sexy lady. I never thought I'd have the chance to play a Cinemax late night movie, but here we are.

Most striking is that the game is very accepting of non-hetero sexuality. The protagonist has a GBF (gay best friend) and he's allowed to express being attracted to him. The GBF isn't a Harvester-style stereotype either. Who knew that a game from the 90s would be so open-minded?

The horror story is fun, with out-of-this-world twists. There's a rat named Blob who sometimes speaks to you. The gialloesque plots are not as predictable as one would expect and it's genuinely sad when someone dies (for the most part). However, this is still an FMV game, so you might not enjoy the gameplay. Thankfully, most of it consists of clicking on areas and backgrounds to progress the story. There's only one endgame puzzle that is overly difficult and nonsensical--be sure to save once you beat it.

Oh, and the OST is vastly better than the original--very moody and atmospheric versus silly chanting/gothic notes.

I would definitely recommend this game if you have mood lighting and a friend to play through it with. If you are a fan of 90s horror like the Silent Night Deadly Night sequels, Cruising, and other such examples, then check this out.

HISTORY

This is an oddity for sure, the unconnected "sequel by name only" to Phantasmagoria 1. The actor playing the protagonist of Curtis Craig - Paul Morgan Stetler - is having a YouTube channel called Conversations with Curtis where he has made interviews with the original cast and crew, as well as an entire let's play of both Phantasmagoria 1 and 2.

This game is notorious for being a dud on release, and later made famous by Noah Antwiler's (Spoony One) early YouTube let's play back in October - December of 2008. It has since had a cult following like most of the FMV - Full Motion Video - games of the 90s.

The genre of FMV was made since CDs were invented and implemented on the console CD-i and later on PC. Going from the floppy disc size of 1.44 MB to the 650 MB of a CD made video possible on computers and consoles for the first time in decent quality. Many games were made in the FMV craze of this time period, and many games had FMV elements in spite of gameplay being separate (games like Wing Commander, Command & Conquer and Jedi Knight).

FMV was replaced by captions with the in game 3D engine instead and has remained so ever since. There's a small subgenre today of FMV games, but it is not a huge hit in spite of some great titles like Her Story and the implementation of FMV in Remedy's Quantum Break. There are more games coming out like The Bunker and Erica, but how these will fair time will tell.

REVIEW

Phantasmagoria 2 has you follow the perspective of Curtis Craig, the single/it's complicated 30-ish Copywriter at a pharmaceutical company. The man has a history of childhood trauma, and hospitalization at a mental institution which becomes apparent in the opening scene.

The game starts out dreadfully boring after the opening scene which can be a turn off for many, but shortly into the boring life a copywriter the first twist comes out of nowhere, and it's all a roller coaster ride from there. You never know what's real in this almost X-Files/psychological thriller which is mixed with lots of sexual themes.

BREAKING GROUND

Phantasmagoria's actors (most of them) are really good. This was filmed during a 6 month period, up to 12 hours a day, and it shows. Most likely a game will never have as many hours and days put into it for a short FMV game like this, I mean the filming was longer than some blockbuster movies!

Curtis has great chemistry with the other characters, and it's easy to like them all. There are explicit sex scenes with nudity and other extreme types of sexual preferences. The game also has an openly gay character who's absolutely amazing! Game studios... what the heck happened?!!!

This is a game from 1996. Again... 1996! Studios today think they are "brave" in games like The Last of Us 2, completely ignoring the work done before. The 90's was a time when barriers where broken constantly and then... something happened? Sales became the most important thing and action and graphics of walls and weapons became more important than pushing boundaries of storytelling.

The game's protagonist's sexuality is also open for debate in many ways, without resorting to being cheesy. Curtis Craig also suffers from deep mental health issues and the stigma of seeking counseling which he finally does. He faces stigma from outsiders, but also receives hopeful comfort and support from friends and lovers. He shares the story of severe childhood trauma and institutionalization, and the impact that has of his life of today. This is a game dealing with very difficult topics that are widely discussed today in 2022 by young and old alike.

VERDICT

Phantasmagoria 2 is an amazing experience. The puzzles are not that hard - except for the notorious final stage. The acting is superb, the quality of video perfectly fine, and you don't have to swap 5 CDs like in the old days. It's soaked in mystery where you wonder what's real or not, and it truly was  a groundbreaking game, way ahead of its time.

I'm not sure if anyone out there is listening, but surely "I heard that Curtis!"

If you clamor for the thrills and chills of being thrust into the amazing world of... sitting in Seattle's crappiest 200 square foot cube farm to solve the nightmarish world of checking emails and punching co-workers' extensions to your touch-tone telephone, then Phantasmagoria 2: A Puzzle of Flesh is the game for you.


I grew up on the PC FMV craze of the 1990s, and far and away Phantasmagoria 2: A Puzzle of Flesh ("Phantas2" from here on out) is the worst of Sierra's triumvirate which also includes the original Phantasmagoria and Gabriel Knight 2: The Beast Within. I am actually a big fan of the FMV "Interactive Movie" style that came out in PC Gaming in the 90s, so it's not that I dislike the genre or the point-and-click style.

Simply put: Phantas2 is boring and claustrophobic. The other two games (Phantas1 and GK2) had charismatic protagonists in Adrienne and Gabriel. Phantasmagoria 1 ropes you in with this gothic horror story and peeking into the history and flashbacks of the Carnovasch mansion. GK2 weaves an historical tale that captivates the audience through the bizarre admixture of Ludwig II, Wagner, and... werewolves. 


Phantas2, by contrast, features Curtis Craig, a 6-foot-tall bespectacled sack of bleh in a personality-less grey t-shirt to match. You're thrust into his world by doing exciting things as:
- Checking your mail
- Finding your wallet
- Using your work ID 
- Checking your email
- Dialing your co-workers' extensions

Riveting. You think the puzzles in point-and-clicks like Phantas1 and GK2 are easy? At least they had puzzles. The majority of Phantas2 is mindlessly mashing about, trying to make sure you clicked on a co-worker (or the world's most aggro sassy black cop trope) enough times to allow you to trigger something fun, like a new .doc to find on your work computer.

When there ARE puzzles, be prepared for worthlessly easy (S&M door puzzle) to "huh?" (RATBOY - a throwaway line given by a coworker once or twice, not repeated, mind). Either way, there is never any payoff, as your reward is another cutscene featuring the community theater-style acting of our intrepid cast.


The graphics in Phantas2 are "better" than its predecessor, in that all is filmed using live sets rather than the previous installment's blue-screen-based world. However, the sets are a detriment to the game's story: the game's big-bad corporate villain has a windowless, 50-square foot office. CEO or janitor's closet? You be the judge. Adrienne's CGI mansion felt like an endless world of possibility compared to Curtis' 4 locations of tiny, dark rooms, and the story in Phantas2 is arguably meant to be something much, much bigger than Adrienne's haunted house story.


So I have to give Phantas2 a big thumbs down, just as I did in the 90s. Even today it holds minimal play appeal. Youtube some of the death scenes for ridiculous camp and spare yourself the anguish of clicking around Seattle's crappiest cube farm for 5 hours.

Das Spiel wirkt zunächst einmal in die Jahre gekommen. 
Aber das ist es ja auch ... immerhin ... 1996.
Dennoch macht es innerhalb der ersten 14 Minuten Spaß. 
OK ... wenig Spielzeit ... ich weiß ... bestimmt folgen Sprüche wie "wie kann man nach so kurzer Zeit ein Urteil bilden?" und ähnliches ... blablabla.
Dennoch kann ich auch nach 14 Minuten sagen dass es für Nostalgiker oder Leute die ein wenig auf den Pfaden der Spielentwicklung wandeln wollen oder Leute die der Melancholie vergangener Tage frönen wollen ein echter Gewinn ist. 

Ich habe damals nur den ersten Teil durchgespielt. 
Der war seiner Zeit ein bahnbrechender Knaller. 
Der zweite Teil im darauf folgenden Jahr ist aus irgendeinem Grund an mir vorbeigegangen!? 
Das Spielprinzip ist jedoch scheinbar das Gleiche. 
Man klickt seinen Spiel-Charakter durch eine Flut von Räumen.
Diese Räume kann man aus verschiedenen Blickwinkeln betrachten.
Somit ist es ein klassisches Adventure das aus einzelnen Bildern aufgebaut ist in denen man die Spielfigur bewegt und mit Objekten und seinem Inventar interagiert. 
Immer wieder zwischendurch wird man mit kurzen Animations-Videos zur Szene belohnt. 

Die Grafik zu seiner Zeit war bahnbrechend. 
Daher ist es für junge und heutige Grafik-Junkies nichts. 
Aber für oben besagte Leute ist es eigentlich ein Muss. 

Schade finde ich das es heute keine solchen Spiele mehr gibt. 
Das letzte vergleichbare Adventure war das Kickstarter geförderte "Tesla Effect" aus der Tex Murphy Reihe. 
Auch hier bei Steam verfügbar und mit wunderschönen 1080P HD Videos gespikt. 
Hier in Phantasmagoria 2 ist die Auflösung natürlich minimal dagegen. 
Dennoch ist das Grundprinzip ähnlich. 
Hinzu kommt das alle Spiele auf dem Markt immer aufwendiger werden von der Grafik her. 
Dennoch sehen diese immerzu nach "gemalten" 3D aus. 
Egal ob Waffen oder Figuren etc. 
Damals dachte man bei Spielen wie diesen wie die Welt wohl in der Zukunft aussehen würde hinsichtlich Videospiele und dergleichen?! 
Leider ist der Traum vom Photorealistischen nie aufgegangen. 
Bei Shootern beispielsweise hat man eine Knarre vor sich ... diese (Siehe Doom Eternal etc.) ist aber immer ein sprichwörtlich bemaltes 3D Modell. 
Warum niemand auf die Idee kommt mal ein Photo als Textur über die Waffen zu legen damit es wie echt aussieht ... oder über die Hände welche die Knarre halten und immer im Blickfeld sind ... ist mir ein Rätsel!?
Es wird immer aufwendiger und detailreicher .... aber es bleibt bei einer gemalten Textur die einfach nach Comic aussieht und nicht wie echt. 
Ebenso bei Charakteren. 
Spiele wie Star Wars Battlefront 2 und Konsorten ... Videosequenzen mit langweiliger bemalten Models die stetig nach 3D aussehen aber nicht nach Photorealismus. 
Irgendwo endete die Entwicklung des Photorealistischen und stagnierte in langweiligem bemalten 3D.
Wieso immer 3D-Ingame-Videos eingebunden werden und keine gefilmten Schauspieler ist mir ein Rätsel. 

Jedenfalls ist Phantasmagoria 1 und in diesem Fall Phantasmagoria 2 noch aus den guten alten Tagen als die Hoffnung und Träume an eine photorealistische Zukunft der spiele noch geträumt wurden. 
Daher von mir her ein klarer Daumen hoch!!!

I played both the first and second Phantasmagoria games in quick succession, and I have to say that this one did not nearly stack up to the first one. And it's a real shame, I wanted to like this one so badly.

PROS:
- Pretty good acting and line delivery.
- Good ambient music.
- Small details like the flashing file names when using the computer subtly up the creep factor.
- Strong opening premise - I was hooked on the plot from the start of the game.
- Trevor
-Blob

CONS:
- I know this is a 90's era Sierra title, but some of the puzzle solutions/progression were really esoteric. The first game presented a pretty clear set of goals: unlock these doors, investigate this noise, etc. It's a bit more vague when the goal is to run the clock on the work day by...showing all your coworkers a picture of your parents?
- The great starting premise that I mentioned earlier? Well there's a hard third-act twist that really jumps the shark in a stupid way, in my opinion. Really left field and doesn't tie up any questions or loose ends. Ultimately, the explanation and final ending just fall flat.
- There's a game-crashing bug that, thankfully, has an easy solution, but if you come across it after a long spell without a save it just doesn't feel worth it to go back.

Unfortunately I'd have to say this game misses the mark. I was really into the first half, forgiving and hopeful the next quarter, and frustrated in the home stretch.
